title: Why Dominant People Get Heard
text:
It is well known that people with dominant personalities tend to gain influence in groups. In 2009 Cameron Anderson and Gavin Kilduff tested why. One explanation is that dominant people simply bully others into going along. The other is that they look more capable than they are.

In one study, students first completed a personality measure of dominance. They were then put into small groups to solve a set of math problems similar to those on graduate admissions tests, and the sessions were recorded. Afterward, group members rated each other's competence and influence, and outside observers rated the video.

Dominant individuals did become more influential, but not because they intimidated anyone. They spoke up first and offered more answers, and they behaved in ways that made them seem competent, which led both teammates and observers to see them as more able. Their actual math ability, measured separately, was no better than anyone else's. In a second study with a different task, the same pattern held: dominant people were seen as more competent even when they were not.
lesson: Confidence and speaking first are easily mistaken for competence. When choosing whom to follow or promote, look at track records, not only at who talks most.
source: Anderson, C., and Kilduff, G. J. (2009). Why do dominant personalities attain influence in face-to-face groups? The competence-signaling effects of trait dominance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 96(2), 491-503.
